subject: Art & Design
title: Hex Codes and RGB: Digital Color Basics
description: A quick, practical guide to Hex Codes and RGB: Digital Color Basics.

hook.text: #FF0000 is pure red. #00FF00 is pure green. Every color on your screen is just six characters.

buildup.text: Hex codes represent RGB values in base-16. Each pair controls red, green, or blue intensity (0-255).

discovery.text: RGB is additive: mixing all channels at full intensity (#FFFFFF) creates white, not black.

twist.text: Two hex codes can look identical on one monitor and different on another. Calibration matters.

climax.text: Design systems use hex codes as a shared language. '#4ECDC4' means the same thing to every developer.

punchline.text: Six characters. 16.7 million possible colors. That's hex.

quiz.question: What does the hex code #FFFFFF represent?

details.summary: Digital colors are defined by mixing red, green, and blue light in values from 0 to 255. Hex codes compress these values into six-character codes — #FF0000 is pure red (255 red, 0 green, 0 blue).
details.whyItMatters: Designers, developers, and anyone working with digital media must speak the language of hex and RGB. Without precise color values, 'make it blue' becomes ambiguous. Hex codes ensure exact color reproduction across screens and software.
takeaways: RGB mixes red, green, and blue light from 0 to 255 each
Hex codes compress RGB into six-character notation like #FF0000
These codes are the universal language of digital color

faq.question: How do you read a hex code?
faq.answer: A hex code like #3A7BF2 splits into three pairs: 3A (red = 58), 7B (green = 123), F2 (blue = 242). Each pair is a hexadecimal number (base-16) representing 0-255 intensity. Higher values mean more of that light color. This example is a medium blue with little red.

faq.question: Will the same hex code look the same on every screen?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Screen calibration, brightness settings, ambient light, and display technology (LCD vs OLED) all affect appearance. Color management profiles help standardize output, but some variation is inevitable. Critical color work requires calibrated monitors.
